extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of English literature and literary criticism; people studying Restoration and early 18th-century drama
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical standards for evaluating Restoration and early-18th-century plays and poetry, focused on qualities such as morality, originality, versification, dialogue, characterization, and stage effect. The page discusses how critics judge dramatists (Wycherley, Congreve, Collier) and their works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral propriety / decency
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of indecency, profaneness, and immoral content in plays and poems (e.g., Wycherley’s 'obscene doggerel' and 'nauseous libertinism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works are censured when they display gross profligacy that offends moral taste; Collier’s Short View is cited as a corrective to 'profaneness and immorality of the English stage.' Examples: turning originally virtuous characters into libertines (Viola → 'a pandar of the basest sort'), and 'the most nauseous libertinism' substituted for purity. Anti-pattern: excusing or protecting indecency because it is 'too filthy to handle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / independence of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the play or poem offers original material or is merely derivative ('scarcely more claim to originality than Terence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong work should provide fresh invention rather than borrow wholesale from earlier sources; Wycherley is criticised for finding hints almost everywhere, with best scenes traced to Calderon, Moliere, Racine, etc. Scoring note: heavy reliance on borrowings counts against originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of dialogue (wit, liveliness, naturalness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The style, liveliness, and wit of dialogue — its capacity to sparkle while remaining appropriate to character ('chief merit... lies in the style of his dialogue').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue that is resplendent with wit and yet preserves a colloquial ease is praised (Congreve). Anti-pattern: witty lines that sacrifice plausibility or make characters speak absurdly; excessive 'liveliness' that undermines dramatic propriety. Example of praise: dialogue that makes even the fool retain a colloquial air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic propriety / plot probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Adherence to plausibility and the proper demands of dramatic composition ('sacrifice dramatic propriety to the liveliness of his dialogue'; 'plot is destitute of interest and of probability').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism targets improbable plots, absurd speeches, and scenes that violate what is reasonable for the characters or the stage. Example anti-pattern: introducing lines or situations so absurd that they break audience belief (quoted absurd lines from Country Wife).

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification and metrical craft
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical quality of verse: versification, cadence, variety of pause, swell, and cadence ('style and versification are beneath criticism'; 'wanted variety of pause, of swell, and of cadence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetry requires refined versification and musicality; poor versification is a ground for severe censure. Examples: Pope’s corrections improving versification; Wycherley’s verses criticized for weak cadence and repetitive phraseology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction, concision, and musicality ('diction and music')
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of words, neatness, compactness, pointed expression, and musical quality of lines ('neat, compact, and pointed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given to diction that is precise and pleasant to the ear without harshness or feeble endings. Anti-pattern: loose, diffuse, or repetitive diction; 'same ideas, and even the same words, came over and over again.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and psychological consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithfulness to a character’s moral and psychological core and avoiding caricature ('Moliere exhibited... a pure and noble mind... Wycherley turned him into a ferocious sensualist').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good characterization preserves the integrity and intended moral stature of figures; bad practice is to distort originals into contrary types (e.g., turning Alceste into a rascal). Scoring note: internal consistency and plausibility of motives and conduct are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity and handling of sources / adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: How an author borrows from earlier works and whether the borrowing preserves or perverts the source ('The Country Wife is borrowed from the Ecole des Maris and the Ecole des Femmes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing is acceptable if transformed with worth; it is censured when the adaptation degrades the original’s moral or artistic intent. Example: stealing Viola from Shakespeare and 'marring' her in the stealing is criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic effect and stagecraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of stage presentation — scenic effect, casting, and the play’s suitability to actors and audience ('Love for Love, superior both in wit and in scenic effect').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play should be constructed to make the most of available performers and stage conditions; good casting and scenic arrangement can heighten success. Anti-pattern: plays that fail to produce effective stage pictures despite good lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot interest and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the plot engages and is believable ('plot is equally destitute of interest and of probability').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges penalize thin or implausible plots—stories should hold interest and present credible action. Example: The Old Bachelor criticized for lack of interest and probability despite strong dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of sound versus sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for meaningful substance over mere sonorous phrasing or technical prettiness ('those who preferred sound to sense' are sneered at).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique favors works that pair agreeable sound with genuine sense; valuing sound alone (versification without thought) is treated as a vice. Scoring note: substance should outweigh ornamental sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of repetition and self-plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality within a single author’s oeuvre — avoiding repeated ideas and wording ('the same ideas, and even the same words, came over and over again').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated phrases or recycled thoughts in short compositions count negatively; freshness within a volume is expected. Example: Wycherley’s verses repeat lines and ideas excessively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral taste and the author's sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral sensibility that an author brings to depiction and tone ('so depraved was his moral taste... he believed that he was producing a picture of virtue... really delineating the greatest rascal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism examines whether an author’s moral judgment distorts representation; a defective moral taste that misapprehends virtue is condemned. Works should reflect a coherent and responsible moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of subject and limits of ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether certain subjects or persons are proper objects of ridicule (Collier’s view that ministers and priests should not be indiscriminately ridiculed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collier contends for restraint: some offices or sacred objects ought to be treated with respect. Critics may disagree about scope, but the choice of target for satire is itself an evaluative criterion; misuse can weaken a piece's moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy of satirical modes and rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of various satirical techniques and the force of indignation or sarcasm ('all the modes of ridicule, from broad fun to polished and antithetical sarcasm, were at Collier’s command').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire ranges from broad humor to polished sarcasm and employs 'rhetoric of honest indignation' when apt. Weak satire either misapplies modes or lacks moral seriousness when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminating and proportionate criticism (meta-criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic’s own prudence: avoiding overreaching charges and distinguishing between dramatist and dramatic personae (Collier sometimes fails to distinguish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good critical practice requires careful discrimination — critic should not attribute to an author what is spoken by a dramatic character, nor overextend charges where not warranted. Anti-pattern: condemning trivial liberties or misattributing theatrical speech to authorial belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical and eloquent force in prose/pamphlets
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity of prose argument to move and persuade ('complete master of the rhetoric of honest indignation'; 'bursts of that peculiar eloquence which comes from the heart').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond logical argument, effective polemic or criticism uses morally charged rhetoric and well-placed eloquence; Collier’s Short View is commended for combining mirth with solemnity and powerful invective where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness to contemporary taste and historical moment
rubrics_metrics.description: How well a work fits or resists the moral and aesthetic climate of its time ('we are one remove further from the Restoration... past the Nadir of national taste and morality').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context matters: some faults are judged especially harshly when the society is moving toward more decorum; critics measure works against contemporary shifts in taste and propriety.
